title: Addressing antimicrobial resistance: Why innovation, access and responsible use must go hand in hand

contentHtml:
Antibiotic therapy is often considered as an integral part of treatment of any bacterial infection. But how often do we think about whether the medicine will work when we need it again? Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is making this a pressing concern. As bacteria develop resistance to medicines meant to kill them, even common infections can become harder to treat and can, in some cases, become life-threatening.

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide was resistant to antibiotics in 2023. The situation is concerning as a Lancet study estimated that, by 2050, 1·91 million global deaths will be directly attributable to AMR, while 8·22 million deaths will be linked to it. India’s National Centre for Disease Control's (NCDC) 2025 surveillance report also describes substantial resistance among bacteria isolated from various samples in participating laboratories.

Advt

These data underline how AMR is narrowing treatment options and serve as a serious warning. When antibiotics lose their effectiveness, infections become harder to manage, particularly in people with weakened immune systems, such as those with cancer or organ recipients. This can result in extended hospital stays, increased healthcare costs and reduced treatment choices. Preserving the effectiveness of antibiotics is therefore a collective responsibility, requiring informed and responsible action from everyone, including patients, healthcare professionals, governments and the pharmaceutical industry.

Moving from policy to practiceThe Indian government has taken some important steps. The National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance 2.0 (2025–2029) brings human health, animal health, agriculture and the environment together under the One Health approach, while encouraging private-sector participation. The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) has updated its treatment guidelines using national resistance data and expert inputs, while NCDC is expanding its surveillance network to identify changing resistance patterns. India is also strengthening its surveillance efforts through the National AMR Surveillance Network (NARS-Net), which monitors nine priority pathogens across designated laboratories to track changing resistance patterns. The next step is implementation by using local resistance data to guide prescriptions, improving access to diagnostic tests and making infection prevention routine across healthcare facilities. Along with this, the government’s Red Line campaign reminds people not to use antibiotics without a doctor's prescription, reinforcing the importance of responsible antibiotic use.

Advt

The pharmaceutical industry’s responsibility must evolveBeyond developing antibiotics, the pharmaceutical industry’s responsibility extends to supporting diagnostics, scientific education, access and responsible manufacturing. For instance, providing hospitals with diagnostic tools for testing antibiotic sensitivity helps doctors identify the most effective treatment and avoid the unnecessary use of stronger antibiotics..7 The 2026 Antimicrobial Resistance Benchmark by the Access to Medicine Foundation recognises the efforts of Indian manufacturers in strengthening hospital diagnostic capacity and engaging with suppliers on responsible wastewater management, an important step in limiting environmental resistance. However, gaps in access and stewardship remain, reminding us that innovation must go hand in hand with availability and responsible use of medicines.

Advt

There are lessons from other countries too. The UK's 2025 progress report recorded 1.1 million fewer antibiotic prescriptions in general practice in England in 2023–24. The UN has set a 2030 target for at least 70% of human antibiotic use to comprise WHO Access-group antibiotics, which are preferred first-line treatments for many common infections and have lower potential to drive resistance.What can each of us do?Everyone has a role in addressing AMR. Never take antibiotics without medical advice, or insist on them for viral infections, or share leftover medicines. Follow prescriptions, ask whether diagnostic tests can guide treatment, practise good hygiene and stay up to date with vaccinations. Healthcare professionals must prescribe responsibly, governments should ensure implementation of action plan, and industry must support innovation, access and responsible manufacturing.

The WHO’s 2026 message, “One Health, one action: Prevent AMR now,” reminds us that resistance crosses boundaries between people, animals and the environment. Antibiotics are an important resource, and safeguarding their effectiveness is a responsibility we all share. The choices we make today will determine whether these life-saving medicines remain effective for generations to come.References:1. World Health Organization.
